summary: This document describes methods for handling Unicode strings that represent usernames and passwords. It replaces the older SASLprep approach from RFC 4013, which was based on Stringprep in RFC 3454, with a more sustainable approach based on PRECIS.

eli5.summary: It sets modern rules for how to treat letters from all the world's languages in logins, so the same name or password always works the same way.

questions: how to handle unicode in passwords
subtitle: The PRECIS rules for handling international usernames and passwords, replacing SASLprep.

tldr.problem: Usernames and passwords now contain characters from every writing system, and a naive comparison can wrongly match look-alike strings (such as a superscript one and the digit one) or fail to match the same name typed in different ways.
tldr.mechanism: It defines three PRECIS profiles: UsernameCaseMapped and UsernameCasePreserved (based on the IdentifierClass) for usernames, and OpaqueString (based on the FreeformClass) for passwords. Each fixes how strings are prepared, enforced and compared.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7613 and replaces the older SASLprep approach of RFC 4013 with PRECIS. It adds migration notes for deployments that used SASLprep.

today: RFC 8265 is a Proposed Standard from October 2017 that obsoletes RFC 7613, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8264 and replaces the SASLprep approach of RFC 4013.

sections.title: Why Usernames and Passwords Need Rules
sections.content:
Usernames and passwords are used everywhere for authentication and authorization, either sent as plaintext (as in the SASL PLAIN mechanism of RFC 4616 and the HTTP Basic scheme of RFC 7617) or fed into a cryptographic algorithm such as a hash (as in SCRAM from RFC 5802 and HTTP Digest from RFC 7616).

RFC 8265 defines rules for strings of Unicode code points that represent usernames and passwords. The rules are profiles of the string classes in the PRECIS framework, RFC 8264. The profiles protect developers from the dangers of full Unicode. For example, treating the superscript one (U+00B9) as equal to the digit one (U+0031) would cause false accepts, and an attacker could spoof an account such as user1@example.com.

The document does not change how existing protocols that use SASLprep handle strings. A community that wants to move to PRECIS must explicitly update its protocol definition, because uncoordinated updates can hurt interoperability and security. The methods are not meant for strings that are not usernames (such as LDAP distinguished names), or for secrets that are not strings, such as keys and certificates.
sections.eli5: If a computer thinks two different-looking names are the same, a trickster could pretend to be you. These rules help the computer be careful about which names and passwords match.

sections.title: How Usernames Are Defined
sections.content:
A username is a string of Unicode code points structured as an ordered sequence of userparts, written in a standard Unicode encoding form such as UTF-8. Each userpart may contain only code points allowed by the PRECIS IdentifierClass, so it is almost entirely letters and digits. A username can be one userpart or several separated by spaces. The ABNF is:

username = userpart *(1*SP userpart)
userpart = 1*(idpoint)

Everything not explicitly allowed in the IdentifierClass is disallowed, including private-use and surrogate code points. Constructions such as user@example.com are still fine. A username MUST NOT be zero bytes long, and that check happens after normalization and mapping.

The RFC gives examples. Valid userparts include juliet@example.com, fussball, fußball and the Greek letters pi and sigma. Not valid are foo bar (a space, though it is a valid username made of two userparts), an empty string, henry followed by the Roman numeral four (U+2163, which has a compatibility equivalent), and the infinity symbol (U+221E). The RFC notes that fussball and fußball are different, so a server may need a registration policy that disallows one if the other exists.
sections.eli5: A username is like a list of simple name pieces joined by spaces. Each piece must be made of plain letters and numbers, with no emoji or special symbols.

sections.title: The Two Username Profiles
sections.content:
There are two username profiles. They are identical except for case handling: UsernameCaseMapped maps uppercase and titlecase code points to lowercase (preferably with the Unicode toLowerCase() operation), while UsernameCasePreserved leaves case alone. Both map fullwidth and halfwidth code points to their decomposition mappings, have no additional mapping rule, apply Normalization Form C (NFC), and apply the Bidi Rule of RFC 5893 to strings with right-to-left code points.

The RFC suggests the case-mapped profile is generally preferable, because not mapping case can cause false accepts and user confusion. Reasons for the case-preserved one include backward compatibility with deployed systems. Since case mapping loses information, implementations SHOULD delay it to the last possible moment, such as a lookup, a comparison, or generating a cryptographic salt.

Preparation applies width mapping and then checks that every code point is allowed by the IdentifierClass. Enforcement prepares the string, then applies case mapping (CaseMapped only), normalization and directionality, and finally checks the result is not zero bytes. Comparison prepares and enforces both strings, and treats them as equivalent if and only if they are an exact octet-for-octet match. An implementation MUST NOT treat a string as conforming or two strings as equivalent before these operations are complete.
sections.eli5: One rule treats big and small letters as the same, and the other keeps them different. Either way, the computer tidies up both names first and then checks that they match exactly.

sections.title: The OpaqueString Profile for Passwords
sections.content:
A password is a string of Unicode code points that conforms to the OpaqueString profile of the PRECIS FreeformClass, written in a standard Unicode encoding form. It MUST NOT be zero bytes long. The RFC explains this is not advice about strength; it prevents an application from accidentally omitting a password when a non-empty input collapses to nothing after canonicalization.

Enforcement applies these rules in order.

  • Width mapping: fullwidth and halfwidth code points MUST NOT be mapped.
  • Additional mapping: non-ASCII spaces (general category Zs, other than SPACE U+0020) MUST be mapped to SPACE.
  • Case mapping: none, because lowercase mapping would cause false accepts and reduce security.
  • Normalization: NFC MUST be applied.
  • Directionality: none. The Bidi Rule would shrink the usable characters and reduce possible entropy, and passwords are rarely displayed.

Comparison again requires an exact octet-for-octet match after preparation and enforcement. The RFC's examples show that correct horse battery staple and its capitalized version are different passwords, that symbols and non-ASCII letters are fine, and that tabs and empty passwords are not allowed.
sections.eli5: A password may use almost any character, and capital letters count. The only tidy-up is turning odd kinds of space into a normal space, so the secret does not depend on a hard-to-type character.

sections.title: Migrating from SASLprep
sections.content:
The rules differ slightly from SASLprep (RFC 4013) but not from RFC 7613. The RFC lists what operators should watch for.

For usernames, SASLprep used Normalization Form KC (NFKC), but the new profiles use NFC and disallow code points with compatibility equivalents, such as long s (U+017F), the Roman numeral four (U+2163) and the fi ligature (U+FB01). Operators may want to search their databases for such names and map them to their equivalents, watching for conflicts like HENRYIV versus HENRY plus the Roman numeral. SASLprep also mapped characters commonly mapped to nothing, so operators may remove code points from the PRECIS M category, such as SOFT HYPHEN (U+00AD). SASLprep allowed uppercase, so the operator can pick either username profile.

For passwords, migration may need no data scrubbing if passwords are not stored in the clear. Moving from NFKC to NFC is probably harmless and may mean fewer false accepts, but some passwords that matched under SASLprep might stop working. User software might also reject code points that SASLprep ignored.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook was a bit different, like changing the rules of a board game. If you run a service, check your old names and passwords to see whether any need fixing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Allowing a wide range of characters in passwords can raise entropy, but the RFC says this should be weighed against the need to reproduce them on different devices and input methods.

Systems that follow modern best practice will not use the plain comparison from the password section. Because they run a cryptographic calculation to verify the password, they prepare the password and enforce the OpaqueString rules first, and then do the calculation.

Comparing identifiers such as SASL simple usernames can lead to false rejects or false accepts, both with security impact, discussed in RFC 6943. The security considerations of RFC 8264 apply to the IdentifierClass and FreeformClass used here, and those of Unicode Technical Standard #39 apply to the use of Unicode code points in usernames and passwords.

Applications can add their own rules, such as length limits, and the RFC notes that applying a profile is not always idempotent. An implementation SHOULD reapply the rules until the output is stable, and reject the input if it is not stable after three additional applications.
sections.eli5: Fancy characters make passwords stronger, but they can be hard to type on some devices. The computer should tidy up a password first and then check it, never guess.
